title: An Interview with Pastor Doug Lehman

## Background and Early Life

Doug Lehman grew up in the Bible Presbyterian Church. He was born in Brazil on a property where he now does ministry. The family came to the United States when Doug was about seven or eight years old in 1975. His father, a pastor, and his family were involved in caring for an orphanage property owned by the Presbyterian Church of Brazil.

Doug has seven sons: Darius, Zayn, Titus, Solomon, Lucas, Roman, and Silas. Darius and Zayn were born in Brazil and grew up with other missionary children. Roman was a small child when the family moved to the field, and Silas was not yet born.

## Conversion Testimony

When asked how he came to believe that Jesus Christ was his savior, Doug responded: "By God's grace, I have one of those super boring testimonies of growing up in a Christian home with a dad who is a pastor. I learned the gospel message and story from the very beginning. I can remember as a little kid praying in my bed and just kind of recycling that prayer often as a young child. The Spirit of God transformed my life. I really don't know exactly when, but there was a constant realization of the importance of God and being His child from the beginning of my recollection."

The congregational leader corrected him: "Tell Pastor Doug how we call this kind of testimony." The response was: "Glorious. Not boring, huh? No, glorious. Yeah, truly."

## Overcoming the Fear of Man

During his middle school, high school, and college years, Doug struggled with fear of men. He shared: "The fear of man was something I hadn't heard about in my background in Brazil. There's not a good biblical background of thought on these issues. Kids grow up with cultural emphasis, even in the church. The first time I heard that my shyness, what you would call social phobia or social anxiety, could have a spiritual component was in college with Wayne Mack."

Wayne Mack wrote books on the fear of man. Doug began to understand during his college years that his love of basketball was deeply connected to seeking glory, honor, and respect from men. He explained: "I loved basketball. All my boys love sports too. I realized much of this was connected to seeking glory and honor and respect of men for my own life, and how I could get that through sports. To make that connection was transformative. I wrote a thesis about how to play sports and think about these issues to the glory of God."

DougDoug emphasized how this struggle became valuable for ministry: "Since I struggled with it, I feel I'm an expert with the fear of man. When counseling others struggling with anxiety, I can connect it with theology. Recently, I counseled a young man in his thirties with a wife and children who had intense struggle with anxiety. He's a deacon in a reformed Presbyterian church. Since he has the fear of the Lord, the first time he heard about connecting it with theology—the fear of man, anxiety, and pride—it just clicked. Decades of drugs and medicines became unnecessary. It was amazing to see someone transformed by God's grace in a session or two."

## Call to Ministry

DougDougdescribed his call to ministry: "Growing up in a Christian home, I was taught about the sovereignty of God and the big God theology that Reformed Presbyterianism teaches. I think it got into my soul at a young age. There wasn't a dramatic moment, but a growing sense of the importance of serving the Lord in ministry."

At The Master's College and Western Form Seminary, Doug discovered biblical counseling. "It was presented to me, and I had never thought about that area. It was almost a lost discipline, even within Reformed churches everywhere. When Pastor Jay Adams led a revival and reawakening to biblical counseling in the church, I connected with it and found it so valuable."

Doug explained his interest: "Psychology is the number one studied discipline in the world because man is interesting and everyone has internal struggles. I would have surely been diagnosed with social anxiety disorder and put on drugs. I consider myself a high-degree case. To see the liberating power of the gospel and how God reaches into the depth level of soul and heart was profoundly interesting to me."

He continued: "I grew up in a Reformed Presbyterian church learning the Westminster Shorter and Larger Catechisms and deep theological thinking. But biblical counseling was a hole in our theology. To have that woken up seemed very important and needy. Even through basketball, I started seeing worship struggles in my own heart. The Lord finally took me out, saying, 'Wake up, son, let me help you overcome this fear of man and this idolatry of man-pleasing.'"

## The Basketball Years and Transition to Full-Time Ministry

Doug was part of the Brazilian national team for the 1996 Atlanta Olympics. He played through the pre-tournament season and was highly skilled. However, at age 25 or 26, he suffered a devastating knee injury during a game in Rio de Janeiro. "Everything I was resting my life on was gone," he reflected. "My fame, my finances, my acceptability—all gone. That's what I put my life effort into."

This injury proved providential for his ministry calling. Doug was doing his master's degree in biblical counseling while playing basketball and working at UPS in the evenings. The knee injury came at just the right time—old enough to go to seminary but not too late with family obligations.

While playing basketball in South Brazil, Doug traveled to different cities with new teams and asked pastors about biblical counseling. "There was no one, no one who had heard of that. They had no clue," he said. "Brazil is huge with a whole in understanding biblical counseling. By and large in the Presbyterian world and conservative Protestant theology, it was a new field. I felt the call even more intensely to publicize these materials there, and that's one of the things I've been able to do."

## Location and Context of Ministry

Doug's ministry is located in northeast Brazil, specifically in Aldeia, near the city of Recife. "We're in the farthest east you can go in the Americas," he explained. "The closest you get to Africa is Brazil. That's why during the Second World War, they built a base there so they could cross the Atlantic quickly. Our city is on the coastal area in the farthest east of South America."

Although only about 10 miles from downtown Recife, travel is difficult. "Traffic is so intense—like the I-5 rush hour getting to Seattle, and that's every day throughout the day. So just traveling 10 miles is a big task."

The property where ministry occurs is in Aldeia, described as more rural with small farms. Unlike Seattle's concentrated high-rise buildings, Brazilian cities have thousands of high rises with most people living in apartments. Doug's family escaped apartment living and now has a house with land.

The property has deep historical significance. Doug's parents cared for an orphanage there when Doug was born. "That's why I'm Brazilian because of that. They came back when I was two or three years old. I didn't grow up with Portuguese, but there were Brazilians living at my dad's house when I was seven or eight. I heard the stories, smells, and flavors of Brazil through those years, which ignited a desire and call to go back."

## Establishing the Soledale Gloria Institute

When Doug arrived at the property as a missionary, the orphanage land was not part of the original vision. However, the land's directors, six business men who held the property in trust, approached him: "You're a missionary born on this land. We're not doing anything with this property. Would it be wonderful to see it used in a good way? Are you interested?"

Dougdiscussed the property stewardship: "They initially offered five years. We argued with them and got it for 15 years to run it and pray through it with PMU. It was a pretty big battle to get everyone to see this could be something good. Maybe they saw my desire, passion, and stubbornness. They came on board. Together with PMU and the Brazilian Presbyterian Church, we stepped out in faith."

Moving with six children to the mission field 14 years ago was extremely expensive. The exchange rate was two to one, but providentially, Brazil's economy tanked after several years. "This actually helped us missionaries financially and gave us much more freedom to move around and get things done."

## The Soledale Gloria Institute of Technology and Theology

The primary ministry on the property is the Soledale Gloria Institute of Technology and Theology. "In the States, it's what you would call a gap year program, which doesn't really exist in that context," Doug explained. "We're bringing something new there."

The program takes twenty young men, ages 18 to 25, selected from pastors all over the country. "Pastors identify committed young men graduating from high school who don't know exactly what they want to do. We receive them through a nomination process where pastors give their approval. It's free to the students."

The curriculum combines intense theological discipleship with practical skills. "One year of intense theological training, and we try to pound it all in. They also learn coding as part of technology training. They're encouraged to go to the mission field, not as pastors, but as supporting cast. If you're coding, you can code from anywhere and work in-country, providing critical mass for pastors planting churches overseas and earning income as well. They're not mandated to that, but they're encouraged. Most of them have a job right after finishing their training."

The program also includes physical labor. "Every day they do an hour and a half of manual labor—this is almost unknown for most Brazilian kids. Kids don't work at all in Brazil. To be able to take care of animals and plant seeds, that's old American work ethic that I learned from my dad growing up. Brazil is a great place for this because it rains and there's sunshine all year round. There's also an hour of weightlifting or sports. It's a very compact year of training."

The results have been remarkable. "While I'm traveling right now, they're doing a reunion of all the guys who've graduated. There are like 90 guys who have gone through the program. Now they're getting married and having kids. It's fun to see them gathering as good godly men who can help bring growth and strengthening to the nation."

## Additional Ministries on the Property

Beyond the institute, the property supports multiple ministry functions. Churches rent the property for weekend events, whether evangelism or strengthening days of fellowship. "We're finally getting to a place where we're moving in the direction of being self-sustaining. For that to happen, we really need it rented out every weekend from Friday to Saturday. We're at about 50 percent of the year now, and it's growing every year."

Doug also conducts pastor training events: "We bring pastors back, especially from the interior and countryside areas where they have a difficult time going to the city. We can house them, train them for a week, give them lots of information and modules they can take back to the interior."

The property hosts multiple camps throughout the year. "We do about six or seven camps, which was the most intense schedule. English camp is very labor-intensive. People from the congregation have volunteered—Abigail is doing a workshop on singing to teach the young men. Leah also runs a cafe there, selling American items like apple pies and cinnamon rolls that people can't get in that culture. People come from the city facing a rough road to get there. She's helping the project significantly with funds."

## Challenges and Sustainability

The ministry faces significant challenges. The roads to the property are rough and unpaved, especially the last two miles. "Bumpy roads mean a new car only lasts about five years. When it rains for months, the roads become full of mud. The last two miles is where we live, so it's constant for us. That's been a challenge."

Despite difficulties, Doug is sustained by a sense of God's calling. "As long as I feel that the Lord is using the ministry in a meaningful way to make impact, I can continue. Missionaries face so many difficulties in so many different areas. Socialism is such a heavy burden, and as director of the project, which is like a business, I see what the people face. It's taxing and almost unbearable if it were just for profit. But we have unique advantages."

Doug noted: "The Lord is providentially helping missionaries in several ways. We can step out of normal financial pressures. And because of providential contacts—my cousin has one of the largest law firms—we have access to solutions that many wouldn't have. We're being used in a unique way. Because of all the hardships, if you don't feel like you're being used, you have to get out quick, because you just melt inside. But when you're feeling used and have opportunity for discipleship and training, you can continue."

## Financial Support and Prayer Requests

The congregation supports Doug and the project with approximately $36,000 annually. Doug expressed deep gratitude: "You guys are definitely sending us support, and it's our main financial support there. This is huge encouragement. When the project doesn't have funds, I can't just say we won't pay workers this month. We have many workers, and I'm responsible for them. So you helping the project helps me face that intense pressure. We're so thankful."

He also appreciated participation beyond finances: "The way you've stepped in to participate—some of the youth have come to Brazil for English camp—is all amazing. The prayers and what you guys already do are the main ways. I couldn't ask for more and wouldn't even desire more. You have a lot of responsibilities here with building, and we're thankful you can keep it up."

Doug raised a specific prayer request: "We recently received another property in Garanhuns when another missionary retired. It's about two and a half to three hours away in the mountains—a beautiful place. But right now it's just an expense. We're trying to get it transferred or sold. Pray for that because it would help us finish some projects on our land and complete some buildings. Also, pray for Pastor Dennis and Lucy, who help with additional support."

## Vision and Future

When asked about lessons learned about Christ through serving in Brazil, Doug reflected: "That's a vast question. The main message is about God's sovereignty and the importance of Christ, His Word, the gospel, and the church for all of life. I've learned the importance of knowing Christ not just for individuals, but for marriages, families, local churches, and beyond."

He continued: "When you go to a different country, you see what you live in—the most blessed, rich, wealthy place in the history of the world. When you step out of that and see burdensome economic situations, you want to help. I see solutions in Christ and the wisdom of Christ. There's an all-encompassing need for the proclamation of Christ and His Word for individuals, cultures, and countries. Thank you for the privilege to do that work and for partnering with us through financial support. You allow us to work and try to bring the Word of Christ to lands that don't have the wealth and riches you enjoy. I hope we don't lose that motivation."

At 53 years old, Doug anticipates continuing the work. "As long as Leah can hang in there with me, I think we have another 12 to 15 years in us."
